Frederick Douglass. A formerly enslaved person who became one of the most influential orators and intellectuals of the nineteenth century, whose powerful speeches and autobiographies exposed the moral bankruptcy of slavery and made him a leading voice in the abolitionist movement. His evolution from escaped slave to statesman and his cogent arguments for human equality made him a foundational figure in American civil rights discourse. He escaped slavery in 1838 after years of brutalization in Maryland. His flight was aided by a free Black woman, Anna Murray, whom he married. In 1852 he delivered the speech "What to the Slave is the Fourth of July?"—a searing indictment of American hypocrisy on freedom and slavery. He published three autobiographies in 1845, 1855, and 1881, narratives that rank among the most powerful American texts, recounting his enslavement, escape, and intellectual awakening. He became a leading abolitionist speaker, touring the United States and Europe and drawing crowds with his eloquence and moral authority. Under Presidents Lincoln, Johnson, and Garfield, he held positions in the federal government, including ambassador to Haiti—the highest offices held by a Black American in the nineteenth century. He advocated not only for ending slavery but for full political and civil equality, including women's suffrage. He spoke at the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848, advocating for women's rights alongside the fight for freedom. Abraham Lincoln valued Douglass as an advisor, though Douglass also criticized him and pushed Lincoln toward emancipation. Like Harriet Tubman, he was a fellow formerly enslaved person who fought for freedom, and they represented different paths—Tubman liberating enslaved people via the Underground Railroad while Douglass wielded the power of words. William Lloyd Garrison was his white abolitionist ally, though they eventually became critics over strategies and women's inclusion. John Brown was a radical abolitionist whom Douglass knew, and they debated Brown's violent tactics.
